usage: Polite-neutral; asking a staff member or attendant where parking is
반말, only to a friend who knows the place
Softer; -하면 돼요 ('where is it OK to park') sounds more natural and less demanding
Ask for the lot itself rather than the action — use when you need directions to the structure
examples: 저기요, 주차 어디에 해요?
Excuse me, where do I park?
Said to a guard or staff as you pull up; 저기요 is the natural attention-getter to a stranger
여기 손님인데 주차 어디에 하면 돼요?
I'm a customer here — where should I park?
손님인데 ('I'm a customer') hints you expect free or validated parking; -하면 돼요 sounds warmer than -해요
A: 식당 이용하면 주차 어디에 해요? 건물 뒤에요? / B: 네, 뒤쪽에 대시면 돼요.
A: If I'm eating here, where do I park? Behind the building? / B: Yes, you can pull in around the back.
대다 ('to pull a car into a spot') is what staff say back to you; recognizing it is essential
nuance: 주차 어디에 해요? is 주차 ('parking', Sino-Korean 駐車) + 어디에 ('at where') + 해요 (polite 'do'), literally 'where do I do parking?' — the everyday way to ask where to leave your car. The particle to lock in is 에 (location of arrival/end-state), NOT 에서: 주차하다 marks the spot you end up at with 에, just like 도착하다 (arrive AT). Many learners say 주차 어디에서 해요? but 에서 is for activity-location, not where you park and stay. A softer, very common variant is 어디에 하면 돼요? ('where is it OK to park?'). The useful contrast: 대다 ('to pull a car in') is what attendants say back — 뒤에 대세요 ('park in the back') — so recognize 대다 even though you ask with 하다. Saying 주차 어디 있어요? is a different, wrong question: it asks where the LOT is, not where you should park your car. To staff always keep 요; drop to 어디에 해? only with a friend. Don't confuse 주차 (parking) with 주유 (refueling) — same first syllable, very different situations.

structuredNuance.t: 주차 ('parking', 駐車) + 어디에 ('at where') + 해요 (polite 'do'), literally 'where do I do parking?' The particle 에 marks the spot you end up at (like 도착하다), so the full, clearer variant is 어디에 하면 돼요? ('where is it OK to park?'). To staff always keep 요; to a friend, 주차 어디에 해?

Use 주차 어디에 해요? arriving at a restaurant, building, or event. It's polite-neutral — fine for staff, attendants, or anyone at the venue. Drop 요 only for friends. For a softer tone with higher-status staff add 혹시: 혹시 주차 어디에 하면 돼요?

주차장 어디예요? asks where the LOT is located (directions to a structure), while 주차 어디에 해요? asks where you should leave your car. Staff often respond with 대다 ('pull a car in'): 뒤에 대세요. Note the difference between the question (하다) and the answer verb (대다).

Two traps: (1) Wrong particle — saying 주차 어디에서 해요? uses 에서 (activity-location) but parking ends at a spot, so 에 is correct. (2) Wrong frame — 주차 어디 있어요? asks where the lot EXISTS, not where you should park. Also don't confuse 주차 with 주유 (refueling).

mistakes: Saying 주차 어디에서 해요? with 에서.
주차하다 marks the spot you end at with 에, not the activity-location 에서. Say 주차 어디에 해요? or 어디에 하면 돼요?. 에서 makes it sound like you're asking where the general activity of parking takes place.
Using 주차 어디 있어요? to ask where to park.
That asks where the parking LOT exists. To ask where YOU should park your car, say 주차 어디에 해요?; to find the lot, say 주차장 어디예요?
Mixing up 주차 and 주유.
주차 is parking a car; 주유 is putting in fuel. 주유 어디에 해요? would be asking where to pump gas. Keep 주차 for parking.

usage: Polite-neutral; checking whether a place has a lot — by phone or at the door
반말, to a friend who has been to the place before
Softer and slightly more deferential with -나요; good when calling ahead
More formal phrasing, seen on booking sites and when calling ahead to a venue
examples: 혹시 주차장 있어요?
Do you happen to have parking?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens the question when calling a restaurant or shop
주차장 있어요? 차 가지고 가도 돼요?
Is there parking? Can I come by car?
차 가지고 가다 ('go bringing a car') is the natural way Koreans say 'come by car' — not 차로 가다
A: 주차장 있어요? / B: 네, 건물 지하에 있어요. 2시간 무료예요.
A: Is there parking? / B: Yes, in the building's basement. Free for 2 hours.
지하 ('basement') and 무료 ('free') are the two answers you're listening for; follow up with 무료예요? if not offered
nuance: 주차장 있어요? is 주차장 ('parking lot', 주차 + 場 'place') + 있어요 ('is there'), the basic feasibility check you do before driving somewhere. 있다 is the existence verb — it literally asks 'does a parking lot exist here?' Crucially, 'is there parking' is NOT the same as 'is it free': many Korean lots exist but charge by the hour, so follow up with 무료예요? ('is it free?') or 주차비 얼마예요? The near-synonym 주차 가능해요? ('is parking possible?', 가능 = 可能) is more formal and appears on booking websites; in spoken conversation 주차장 있어요? is friendlier. In quick speech natives drop the subject particle and say 주차장 있어요, not 주차장이 있어요 — keeping 이 sounds overly bookish at a counter. A common error is saying 주차 있어요? without 장 — 주차 alone is the act of parking, so you need the place noun 주차장 to ask about a lot. And when the lot is full, the question shifts to 자리 있어요? ('is there a space?', 자리 = 'spot/seat').

structuredNuance.t: 주차장 ('parking lot', 주차 + 場 'place') + 있어요 ('is there'), asking whether a parking lot exists at this location. 있다 is the existence verb; this is a yes/no feasibility check. In fast speech the subject particle 이 is dropped: 주차장 있어요, not 주차장이 있어요.

Use it before driving to a restaurant, venue, or building — either by phone (add 혹시 to soften) or at the entrance. Polite-neutral 있어요? suits staff and strangers. Drop 요 for friends. 주차장 있나요? is slightly more deferential, good for calling a hotel or clinic.
주차 가능해요? ('is parking possible?', 가능 = 可能) is more formal, seen on booking sites. In casual speech 주차장 있어요? is warmer. When the lot exists but may be full, switch to 자리 있어요? ('is there a space?').
주차장 있나요? (deferential), 주차 가능해요? (formal), 주차 무료예요? (checking if it's free). Smart follow-up after a yes: 몇 시간 무료예요? ('how many hours free?') or 주차비 얼마예요?
Two traps: (1) 주차 있어요? without 장 — 주차 is the act, not the place; you need 주차장. (2) Assuming 'there is parking' means it's free — confirm with 무료예요? or 주차비 얼마예요? after getting a yes.

mistakes: Saying 주차 있어요? without 장.
주차 alone is the act of parking; the place is 주차장. To ask if a venue has a lot, say 주차장 있어요? — dropping 장 sounds unfinished and confusing.
Assuming 'there is parking' means it's free.
Many Korean lots exist but charge by time. After 주차장 있어요?, always confirm cost with 무료예요? ('is it free?') or 주차비 얼마예요?
Forcing 주차장이 있어요? in casual speech.
The subject particle 이 is usually dropped in spoken questions: 주차장 있어요? Keeping 이 isn't wrong but sounds bookish and slightly stiff at a front desk.

usage: Polite-neutral elliptical request; the standard one-word line at a full-service gas station
Please fill it all the way
Fuller, very explicit version — clearer if the attendant looks uncertain
넣다 ('to put in') is the most literal 'fill it up'; equally natural as 채우다
The alternative: buy a fixed won-amount instead of a full tank — very common in Korea
examples: 휘발유 가득이요.
Regular gas, fill it up.
Name the fuel type (휘발유 = gasoline) FIRST, then 가득이요 — the order matters for safety
가득이요. 카드로 할게요.
Fill it up. I'll pay by card.
Stating payment method right away saves an exchange; 카드로 ('by card') is the normal choice
A: 경유 가득 넣어 주세요. 영수증도 주세요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요.
A: Fill it up with diesel, please. And a receipt too. / B: Yes, one moment.
경유 ('diesel') vs 휘발유 ('gasoline') — say the right word for your car; putting diesel in a petrol car causes serious damage
nuance: 가득이요 is 가득 ('full, to the brim') + 이요 (polite ender), an elliptical 'full, please' — the classic line at a 주유소 (gas station) when you want a full tank. The verb (채우다/넣다 'to fill/put in') is understood from context; the full forms 가득 채워 주세요 and 가득 넣어 주세요 are equally natural and clearer if the attendant misses the short version. The critical contrast is full-tank vs. fixed-amount: instead of 가득이요 you can order by won — 삼만 원어치요 ('30,000 won's worth') or 오만 원어치요 — where the suffix -어치 means 'worth of', turning a money amount into a fuel quantity. This is extremely common in Korea and surprises English speakers. You MUST name your fuel type before 가득이요: 휘발유 (gasoline/petrol), 경유 (diesel), or 고급 (premium). A pitfall is saying 가득 주세요 — 주다 ('give') is fine but slightly odd since it wants a thing to give; 채워/넣어 주세요 fits 'fill' better. At 셀프 주유소 (self-service stations) you won't say any of this to an attendant — you operate the pump screen yourself.

structuredNuance.t: 가득 ('full, to the brim') + 이요 (polite ender) — an elliptical 'full, please', with the verb (채우다/넣다) omitted because context makes it clear. Full forms: 가득 채워 주세요 / 가득 넣어 주세요. At 셀프 주유소 you operate the pump yourself, so this is for attended stations only.

Said to an attendant at a full-service 주유소 as you pull in. The 이요 ending is polite-neutral — appropriate for any attendant. You can drop to 가득이요 (same word, 이요 already there) or raise to 가득 채워 주세요 for clarity. Never drop the ender entirely: bare 가득 sounds abrupt.

가득이요 (full tank) vs 삼만 원어치요 (fixed amount). -어치 means 'worth of': 오만 원어치 = 50,000 won's worth of fuel. Fixed amounts are very common since drivers on a budget avoid overfilling. Don't say 가득 주세요 — 주다 ('give') wants a countable thing; use 채워/넣어 주세요 for 'fill'.
가득이요 → 가득 채워 주세요 → 휘발유 가득 넣어 주세요. For fixed amounts: 이만 원어치요 / 삼만 원어치요 / 오만 원어치요.

Two traps: (1) Forgetting to name the fuel type — 가득이요 alone doesn't say petrol or diesel; always lead with 휘발유 or 경유. (2) Not knowing about 원어치 orders — English speakers default to 'fill it up' but fixed-won orders are equally common and useful in Korea.

mistakes: Saying just 가득 with no ending to an attendant.
Bare 가득 sounds abrupt. Add the polite 이요 (가득이요) or use a full verb: 가득 채워 주세요 / 가득 넣어 주세요.
Forgetting to state the fuel type.
가득이요 alone doesn't specify gasoline or diesel. Lead with 휘발유 가득이요 or 경유 가득이요 — putting diesel in a petrol car causes serious engine damage.
Using -어치 wrong for a fixed amount.
'30,000 won's worth' is 삼만 원어치요, not 삼만 원요 alone. The suffix -어치 ('worth of') is what turns the money amount into a fuel quantity.

usage: Polite-neutral; telling a passenger you must stop to refuel
반말, to a close friend riding with you
주유하다 is the formal Sino-Korean verb for the same act; sounds like a news bulletin or formal notice
Explaining the WHY — the tank is nearly empty; a softer, more descriptive framing
examples: 잠깐만요, 기름 넣어야 돼요.
Hold on, I need to get gas.
Said mid-drive before pulling into a station; 잠깐만요 warns passengers of a detour
기름 넣어야 돼서 주유소 좀 들를게요.
I need gas, so I'll stop by a station.
들르다 ('to stop by briefly') is the natural verb for a quick gas stop — not 가다 or 방문하다
A: 기름이 거의 없어서 기름 넣어야 돼요. 근처에 주유소 있어요? / B: 저기 편의점 옆에 있어요.
A: I'm low on gas so I need to fill up. Is there a station nearby? / B: There's one next to that convenience store over there.
Pair the need with asking 근처에 주유소 있어요? ('is there a station nearby?') for the natural two-step exchange
nuance: 기름 넣어야 돼요 is 기름 ('oil/fuel', the everyday spoken word for car fuel) + 넣다 ('to put in') + -어야 되다 ('have to'), literally 'I have to put fuel in' — the casual, most common way to say 'I need to get gas.' 기름 literally means 'oil' but in a car context everyone understands it as gasoline; the formal Sino-Korean counterpart is 주유하다 (注油 'pour fuel'), which you see on 주유소 signs. The verb to fix in memory is 넣다 ('put in') because you put fuel INTO the tank — a typical error is 기름 사야 돼요 ('have to BUY gas'), but Koreans frame this as putting it in, not purchasing it. For the ending, -어야 돼요 and -어야 해요 both mean 'have to'; 돼요 (from 되다) is the more conversational spoken choice. The biggest English-speaker trap is calling car fuel 가스 — in Korean 가스 means cooking gas or LPG, so 가스 넣어야 돼요 sounds like you're filling a gas canister, not a car tank. Use 기름 or 휘발유/경유 for a car. To a friend, 기름 넣어야 돼.

structuredNuance.t: 기름 ('oil/fuel') + 넣다 ('to put in') + -어야 되다 ('have to') — literally 'I have to put fuel in.' 기름 means 'oil' but car context makes 'gasoline/fuel' clear to everyone. The verb is 넣다 (put in), not 사다 (buy) — Koreans frame refueling as putting fuel into the tank, not buying it.

Said to passengers in your car, or to yourself aloud while driving. Polite with 돼요, casual with 돼 (반말). Pair with 주유소 들를게요 ('I'll stop at a station') to make it a complete heads-up. The formal 주유해야 돼요 fits written notices or intercom announcements, not casual car conversation.

주유해야 돼요 (formal, Sino-Korean 注油) vs 기름 넣어야 돼요 (casual, everyday). 기름이 거의 다 됐어요 ('almost out') is softer — it describes the state rather than asserting the need. -어야 돼요 vs -어야 해요: both mean 'have to'; 돼요 is more conversational.
기름 넣어야 돼요 → 기름 좀 넣어야 될 것 같아요 (softer hedge) → 기름이 거의 없어서 주유소 들러야 돼요 (fuller explanation).
Two traps: (1) 가스 넣어야 돼요 — 가스 means cooking/LPG gas in Korean, not car fuel. Car fuel is 기름 (casual) or 휘발유/경유 (specific). (2) 기름 사야 돼요 — Koreans frame refueling as 넣다 ('put in'), not 사다 ('buy').

mistakes: Saying 기름 사야 돼요 ('I have to buy gas').
Koreans frame refueling as 넣다 ('put in'), not 사다 ('buy'). Say 기름 넣어야 돼요. 사야 돼요 sounds like buying bottled oil off a shelf.
Calling gasoline 가스.
가스 means cooking/LPG gas in Korean. Car fuel is 기름 (or 휘발유/경유 for the specific type). 가스 넣어야 돼요 sounds like refilling a gas canister, not a fuel tank.
Using the wrong particle: 기름에 넣어야 돼요.
기름 is the thing you put in (object), so it takes 을/를 or no particle: 기름(을) 넣어야 돼요. 기름에 would mean 'put something INTO the oil'.

usage: Polite-neutral; checking if you pump your own gas before you pull up to a pump
반말, to a friend who may know the station
Fuller version naming 주유소 ('gas station') — clearer when asking at a distance or by phone
The opposite question — asking if staff pump for you at a full-service station
examples: 여기 셀프예요?
Is this self-service here?
Asked as you pull in, scanning the pumps and unsure which type it is
A: 셀프예요? / B: 네, 저기 화면에서 선택하시면 돼요.
A: Is it self-serve? / B: Yes, just make your selection on that screen over there.
The attendant will direct you to the screen — listen for 선택하다 ('to select') and 결제하다 ('to pay')
셀프 주유소가 더 싸요. 직접 넣어야 되지만요.
Self-service stations are cheaper, though you pump it yourself.
직접 넣다 ('pump it yourself', 직접 = 'directly/in person') — self-serve trades effort for a lower price, often by 50–100 won per liter
nuance: 셀프예요? is the loanword 셀프 (from English 'self-service') + 예요 (polite copula), 'is it self-service?' Korean gas stations divide sharply into 셀프 주유소 (you pump, cheaper) and 일반/풀서비스 stations where a 직원 (attendant) does it; 셀프 stations are now the majority and clearly cheaper, so this question has real money consequences. 셀프 functions as a standalone noun/adjective in Korean far beyond English: 셀프 세차 (self car-wash), 셀프 계산대 (self-checkout counter), 셀프 촬영 (self-photography booth) — so 셀프예요? fully means 'is it self-service?' without further explanation. The copula after a vowel-final noun is 예요 (NOT 이에요): 셀프 ends in a vowel, so 셀프예요, never 셀프이에요. At a 셀프 station you interact with a screen: select 휘발유/경유, choose amount (가득 or a won amount), prepay by card or cash, then pump. The English-speaker trap is over-explaining with 제가 직접 해야 돼요? ('do I have to do it myself?') — that works but 셀프예요? is crisper and exactly what locals say.

structuredNuance.t: 셀프 (English loan 'self-service') + 예요 (polite copula after vowel-final noun), 'is it self-service?' The copula rule: vowel-final noun + 예요 (NOT 이에요). At a 셀프 station you interact with a touchscreen — select fuel type, amount, prepay, then pump yourself.

Ask as you pull in or before leaving your car. Polite-neutral 예요? to staff or anyone nearby. To a friend, 셀프야? The opposite question — 직원이 넣어 줘요? — is for confirming full-service if you prefer someone else to pump.

셀프 (pump yourself, cheaper) vs 일반/풀서비스 (attendant pumps, slightly pricier). 직접 넣다 ('pump it yourself', 직접 = in person/directly) is the verb for what you do at a 셀프 station. Don't confuse 셀프 (self-serve) with 무인 ('unmanned') — 셀프 still has staff around to help; 무인 means no staff at all.
여기 셀프예요? → 여기 셀프 주유소예요? → 직원이 넣어 줘요, 아니면 셀프예요?
Two traps: (1) 셀프이에요? — wrong copula form; after a vowel, it's 예요, giving 셀프예요. (2) Over-explaining with 제가 직접 해야 돼요? — perfectly understandable but verbose; 셀프예요? is the native, one-word check.

mistakes: Saying 셀프이에요? after the vowel.
셀프 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 예요: 셀프예요? 셀프이에요 is the wrong form for a vowel-final noun.
Thinking 셀프 needs an English-style full phrase.
In Korean 셀프 stands alone as 'self-service'. You don't need 셀프 서비스예요?; 셀프예요? is complete and natural.
Confusing 셀프 (self-serve) with 무인 (unmanned).
셀프 means you pump it yourself, usually with staff around to help. 무인 ('unmanned') means no staff at all. They overlap but aren't identical; ask 셀프예요? for the pump-it-yourself question.

usage: Polite; telling a driver the signal has turned green — the nudge from the passenger seat
반말, to a friend who is driving and may be distracted
Naming the color directly rather than the change — stating the current state
The stop version — 빨간불 ('red light'); used as a warning to a distracted driver
examples: 신호 바뀌었어요, 가도 돼요.
The light changed — you can go.
Tell the driver it's green AND confirm it's safe; 가도 돼요 ('it's OK to go') is the reassurance
앞에 빨간불이에요, 멈춰야 돼요.
Red light ahead — you need to stop.
멈추다 ('to stop/brake') paired with 빨간불 for a direct warning
A: 신호 바뀌었어요! / B: 어? 뒤에서 빵빵거려요.
A: The light changed! / B: Huh? They're honking behind us.
빵빵거리다 ('to honk repeatedly') is what other drivers do when you miss a green — the sound is 빵빵
nuance: 신호 바뀌었어요 is 신호 ('signal/traffic light', Sino-Korean 信號) + 바뀌다 ('to change/switch') in polite past, 'the light has changed' — what a passenger says to nudge a driver, typically meaning it turned green. 신호 alone means the traffic signal in driving context; the full form is 신호등 ('signal lamp', 등 = 燈 'light'). Essential color vocab: 빨간불 (red), 초록불 (green) — but crucially, Koreans commonly say 파란불 ('blue light') for green. This is not a mistake; it's standard usage rooted in how Korean historically categorized color. Never 'correct' it. The verb 바뀌다 is intransitive ('it changes by itself'), distinct from transitive 바꾸다 ('to change something'): a light 바뀌다 on its own; someone 바꾸다 a channel. Saying 신호 바꿨어요 wrongly implies a person changed it. Also distinguish 신호 ('traffic light/signal') from 표지판 ('road sign') — a stop sign or speed limit sign is 표지판, not 신호. And 신호위반 ('running a red', 위반 = violation) is the serious offense. To a friend, 신호 바뀌었어.

structuredNuance.t: 신호 ('traffic signal', 信號) + 바뀌다 (intransitive 'to change by itself') in polite past — 'the light has changed.' 신호 alone is the signal; 신호등 is the full 'signal lamp' (등 = 燈). Colors: 빨간불 (red), 초록불 / 파란불 (green — Koreans commonly say 파란불 'blue' for green, and this is standard, not an error).

Said by a passenger to a driver who has missed or is about to miss a light. Polite with 바뀌었어요; 반말 바뀌었어 to friends. For urgency, 신호 바뀌었어요! with rising intonation. The opposite is 아직 빨간불이에요 ('still red') to hold back an eager driver.

바뀌다 (intransitive, the light changes itself) vs 바꾸다 (transitive, someone changes something). 신호 바뀌었어요 vs 신호 바꿨어요: the second wrongly implies a human changed it. Distinguish 신호 ('traffic light') from 표지판 ('road/warning sign'): you 신호위반 (run a red), you don't '표지판위반'.
신호 바뀌었어요 → 초록불이에요, 가도 돼요 → 신호 언제 바뀌어요? (when does it change?) → 신호위반하면 안 돼요 (don't run the red).

The key error is 신호 바꿨어요 — using transitive 바꾸다 implies a person changed the signal, which is nonsensical; use intransitive 바뀌다. Also, mixing 신호 (a light/signal) with 사인 (a signature/cue) or 표지판 (a sign): road SIGNS are 표지판, not 신호.

mistakes: Saying 신호 바꿨어요 instead of 바뀌었어요.
바꾸다 is transitive ('to change something'); 바뀌다 is intransitive ('it changes'). A traffic light changes on its own, so 신호 바뀌었어요. 바꿨어요 wrongly says someone changed it deliberately.
Assuming 파란불 is literally a blue light.
Koreans commonly call the green go-signal 파란불 ('blue light'). It means GREEN — this is standard usage, not an error. Both 파란불 and 초록불 are acceptable; don't 'correct' either.
Using 사인 or 신호 for a road sign.
신호 is a traffic signal/light; 사인 is a signature or hand-cue. A street SIGN (stop sign, speed-limit marker) is 표지판. Keep 신호 for the lights only.

usage: Polite imperative; telling an adult passenger to buckle up
반말, to a close friend or a child
Shortened — 벨트 alone is fully understood in a car context; very common
The consequence — 벌금/과태료 ('fine') if you don't buckle; said to a reluctant passenger
examples: 출발할게요, 안전벨트 매세요.
I'm setting off — please buckle up.
출발하다 ('to depart/set off') then the seatbelt reminder: the natural pre-drive sequence
뒷자리도 안전벨트 매세요. 단속해요.
Buckle up in the back too. They enforce it.
단속하다 ('to crack down/enforce') — police actively check rear seatbelts; fines apply to ALL seats
A: 애기는 카시트에 앉히고 안전벨트 매 주세요. / B: 네, 딸깍 됐어요.
A: Put the baby in the car seat and buckle them in. / B: OK, it clicked in.
앉히다 ('to seat someone') + 카시트 ('car seat'); 딸깍 is the click sound confirming the belt is locked
nuance: 안전벨트 매세요 is 안전벨트 ('seatbelt', 안전 'safety' 安全 + 벨트 'belt') + 매다 ('to fasten/tie') in polite imperative, 'please fasten your seatbelt.' The critical verb is 매다 ('to tie/fasten') — the same verb used for tying a necktie (넥타이 매다). Common errors are 안전벨트 하세요 (too vague) or 끼세요 (끼다 is 'to insert/put on glasses', wrong for a belt). In Korea all passengers including back-seat riders must buckle by law; 벌금 or 과태료 (fines) apply to everyone, and police do conduct enforcement campaigns, so 뒷자리 passengers are expected to buckle too. To undo the belt on arrival: 풀다 ('to undo/unfasten') — 벨트 푸세요. 안전벨트 is often clipped to 벨트 in everyday speech. The English-speaker trap beyond the verb is 입다 ('to wear' clothes) — you don't 입다 a belt, you 매다 it. Also be careful not to confuse 매다 ('fasten') with the identically pronounced 메다 ('to carry on the shoulder', as in 가방 메다 'sling a bag') — same sound, different verb.

structuredNuance.t: 안전벨트 ('seatbelt', 安全 'safety' + 벨트 'belt') + 매다 ('to tie/fasten') in polite imperative. 매다 is the same verb as tying a necktie: 넥타이 매다. The opposite on arrival is 풀다 ('to undo'): 벨트 푸세요. 안전벨트 often shortens to 벨트 in speech.

Said to passengers before setting off, or to a child or friend. Polite imperative 매세요 to adult passengers; 매 (반말) to kids or close friends; the favor form 매 주세요 sounds gentler if you are asking rather than instructing. It is a normal, expected instruction — not nagging — since all seats are legally required.
안전벨트 매세요 (direct imperative) vs 안전벨트 매 주세요 (favor/softer request). Don't confuse 매다 ('fasten belt') with 메다 ('carry on shoulder', 가방 메다) — same pronunciation, different verbs with different objects.
매세요 → 매 주세요 → 꼭 매세요 ('make sure to buckle') → 뒷자리도 매세요. Opposite: 다 왔어요, 벨트 푸세요.

Two verb errors: (1) 안전벨트 하세요 — 하다 is too generic; use 매다. (2) 안전벨트 입으세요 — 입다 is for clothing; a belt is tied/fastened with 매다. Also note 매다 (fasten) and 메다 (shoulder-carry) sound identical — context and object distinguish them.

mistakes: Saying 안전벨트 하세요 or 끼세요.
A seatbelt is fastened with 매다: 안전벨트 매세요. 하다 is too generic and 끼다 ('to insert/put on glasses') is the wrong verb for a belt.
Using 입다 ('to wear') for a seatbelt.
입다 is for clothing. A belt is tied/fastened: 매다. So it's 안전벨트 매세요, never 안전벨트 입으세요.
Confusing 매다 (fasten) with 메다 (carry on shoulder).
They sound the same but 매다 = fasten a belt/tie, 메다 = sling a bag over your shoulder. For a seatbelt use 매다: 벨트 매세요.

usage: Polite; telling a taxi driver or any driver where to let you out
반말, to a friend driving — only to someone you are close with
Passenger announces own action rather than instructing the driver; slightly softer
저 앞에서 ('just ahead there') fine-tunes the exact spot without naming a landmark
examples: 여기 세워 주세요.
Please stop here.
Standard line to a taxi driver at your destination — concise and clear
저 횡단보도 앞에서 세워 주세요.
Please pull over before that crosswalk.
횡단보도 ('crosswalk') as a landmark; cars cannot legally stop ON a crosswalk
A: 여기 잠깐 세워 주세요. 금방 올게요. / B: 네, 비상등 켜고 기다릴게요.
A: Pull over here a sec — I'll be right back. / B: OK, I'll put the hazards on and wait.
잠깐 ('for a moment') + 금방 올게요 ('back soon'); 비상등 켜다 ('turn on hazard lights') is what the driver naturally does for a brief stop
nuance: 여기 세워 주세요 is 여기 ('here') + 세우다 ('to make stop / bring to a halt') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor'), 'please stop the car here.' The verb is causative 세우다 ('to make X stand/stop'), distinct from intransitive 서다 ('to stop, of itself'). You ask the driver to 세우다 the car; you say a person 서다 ('stands'). The classic learner error 여기 서 주세요 wrongly tells the driver to personally stand. The particle on the location is usually 에서 contracted to 서 in speech: 저 앞에서 세워 주세요 ('pull over at that point up ahead'). The passenger-twin expression is 여기서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off here', 내리다 = 'to get out/off a vehicle') — it's your own action announced, not an instruction. For a taxi, both work but 여기 세워 주세요 is more direct. The English-speaker trap is using 멈추다 ('to halt/cease motion') — 멈추다 is for motion stopping abruptly, not a graceful pull-over; 세우다 ('pull over and park momentarily') fits. Also don't use the formal 정지해 주세요 ('please stop', 정지 = the stop-sign word) — it's stiff and sign-like for a human driver. To a friend, 여기 세워 줘.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 세우다 (causative 'to make stop/stand') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor') — 'please stop the car here.' 세우다 is causative; you are making the car stop. The intransitive pair is 서다 ('to stop/stand by itself'). Location particle: 에서/서 because stopping is an action AT a spot — 저 앞에서 세워 주세요.

Said to taxi drivers, private drivers, or anyone driving you. Polite with 주세요 — appropriate for any driver. 여기서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off here') is the softer passenger-side equivalent, announcing your own action. To a friend, 여기 세워 줘.

여기 세워 주세요 (instructing the driver) vs 여기서 내릴게요 (announcing your own exit). Both land you in the same place but the framing differs. Don't use 멈춰 주세요 (too abrupt, signals sudden stop) or 정지해 주세요 (traffic-sign register, sounds like a police command).
여기 세워 주세요 → 저 앞에서 세워 주세요 → 저 건물 앞에서 세워 주세요 → 잠깐 세워 주세요, 금방 올게요.

Two errors: (1) 여기 서 주세요 — intransitive 서다 means 'you yourself stand here', not 'stop the car here'; you need causative 세우다. (2) 멈춰 주세요 / 정지해 주세요 — too abrupt or too sign-like; 세워 주세요 is the natural pull-over request.

mistakes: Saying 여기 서 주세요 with intransitive 서다.
서다 ('to stand/stop oneself') would tell the driver to personally stand here. You want the causative 세우다 ('make the car stop'): 여기 세워 주세요.
Using 멈춰 주세요 to mean 'pull over'.
멈추다 is 'to halt/cease' and sounds like an emergency stop. To have a taxi let you out gracefully, say 여기 세워 주세요; 멈추다 is more for stopping motion suddenly or pausing a machine.
Saying 정지해 주세요.
정지 is the formal 'STOP' on signs and signals. As a request to a taxi driver it's stiff and strange. Use the everyday 세워 주세요.

english: The traffic is bad / the road is jammed
usage: Polite-neutral; describing current heavy traffic to a passenger or someone you're calling
반말, to a friend — often said to explain why you're late
차가 막히다 ('cars are jammed') with surprised -네요; slightly more emphatic
The opposite — 뻥 뚫리다 ('to open up completely'); 뻥 is an expressive adverb meaning 'wide/suddenly clear'
examples: 지금 길이 막혀요. 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
The roads are jammed right now. I might be a bit late.
Pair with 좀 늦을 것 같아요 ('I might be a bit late') — the natural follow-up when explaining a delay
퇴근 시간이라 길이 많이 막혀요.
It's rush hour so traffic is really heavy.
퇴근 시간 ('leaving-work time') = evening rush hour; 출근 시간 ('going-to-work time') = morning rush
A: 사고 났나 봐요, 길이 너무 막혀요. / B: 다른 길로 가 볼게요.
A: Looks like there was an accident — traffic's terrible. / B: I'll try another route.
사고 나다 ('an accident happens') with -나 봐요 for a guess; 다른 길로 ('via another road') is the natural response
nuance: 길이 막혀요 is 길 ('road/way') + 이 (subject) + 막히다 ('to be blocked/clogged') in polite present, 'the road is jammed.' 막히다 is the intransitive/passive of 막다 ('to block') — the road IS blocked by traffic — so the subject is the road or the cars: 길이 막히다 or 차가 막히다, both completely standard. The natural opposite is 뚫리다 ('to be unclogged, flowing freely'): 길이 뻥 뚫렸어요, where 뻥 is an expressive adverb meaning 'wide open.' The English-speaker trap is calquing 'there is traffic' as 교통이 많아요 or 트래픽이 있어요 — 교통 (交通) means 'transportation' as a system, not a jam, so 교통이 많아요 sounds odd; use 막히다. The other trap is using transitive 막다: 길을 막아요 means YOU are blocking the road. For the noun 'traffic jam' Koreans say 교통 체증 or 차 막힘, but the practical verb sentence is always 막히다. Register: 막혀요 is polite-neutral; drop 요 to a friend. Tenses: 막혀요 (currently jammed), 막혔어요 (was/got jammed), 막힐 거예요 (will be jammed — useful when asking about rush hour).

structuredNuance.t: 길 ('road') + 이 (subject) + 막히다 (intransitive 'to be blocked') in polite present — 'the road is jammed.' 막히다 is the intransitive/passive of 막다 ('to block'): the road is blocked BY traffic. Both 길이 막히다 and 차가 막히다 are standard. Opposite: 뻥 뚫리다 ('to open wide', 뻥 = expressive 'all the way open').

Used when explaining lateness (길이 막혀서 늦었어요), warning a driver (막힐 것 같아요 — 'it'll probably be jammed'), or chatting about a commute. Polite 막혀요 for most contexts; 막혀 (반말) to close friends. -네요 (차가 많이 막히네요) adds mild surprise.

막히다 (intransitive, road/cars are jammed) vs 막다 (transitive, someone blocks something): 길을 막아요 means YOU are blocking it. The noun form is 교통 체증 ('traffic jam', formal) or 차 막힘 (casual). Don't use 교통이 많아요 — 교통 (交通) is the traffic system, not a jam.
막혀요 (now jammed) → 막혔어요 (was jammed) → 막힐 거예요 (will be jammed) → 너무 막혀서 못 가겠어요 ('so jammed I can't go').
Two traps: (1) 길을 막아요 (transitive) means YOU block the road, not that the road is jammed — use 길이 막혀요 (intransitive). (2) 교통이 많아요 / 트래픽이 있어요 — unnatural translations; Koreans say the road/cars 막히다.

mistakes: Saying 길을 막아요 ('I block the road').
막다 is transitive ('to block something'); the road being jammed is intransitive 막히다. Say 길이 막혀요. 길을 막아요 means you are physically obstructing it.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for heavy traffic.
교통 means 'transportation/traffic' as a system, not a jam. 'Traffic is heavy' is 길이/차가 막혀요. 교통이 많아요 sounds unnatural.
Using 막혀요 for a clogged drain only.
막히다 covers both a jammed road and a blocked pipe/nose. In a driving context 길이 막혀요 clearly means a traffic jam — context, not a different verb, distinguishes them.

usage: Polite; asking a passenger to punch the destination into the navigation screen
반말, to a friend in the passenger seat while you keep your eyes on the road
Please enter the address in the GPS
Fuller version spelling out 주소 ('address') — useful when you're about to dictate the address
Just powering it on (켜다 = 'to turn on') — said when the screen is off
examples: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요. 주소 불러 드릴게요.
Set the GPS, please — I'll read out the address.
불러 드리다 ('read aloud for you') as you dictate; this two-step is the natural flow
A: 내비 찍어 봤어요? 몇 분 걸려요? / B: 한 35분 걸린대요.
A: Did you set the nav? How long does it say? / B: It says about 35 minutes.
찍어 보다 ('try setting it') then ask the ETA — 걸린대요 ('it says it takes') uses reported speech
내비대로 가면 돼요. 곧 우회전이래요.
Just follow the nav — it says right turn soon.
내비대로 ('according to the nav', -대로 = 'as per') + 우회전 ('right turn'); -이래요 is reported speech from the nav
nuance: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 is 내비 (clipped from 내비게이션 'navigation', i.e. car GPS) + 좀 (softener, makes the request gentler) + 찍다 ('to punch in / tap / mark a point') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor'), 'please punch the destination into the GPS.' The key word is 찍다: its core sense is 'to stamp/press/tap,' and Koreans use it for tapping entries on screens — 주소를 찍다 ('punch in the address'), 목적지를 찍다 ('tap in the destination'), 점을 찍다 ('mark a point on a map'). English speakers reach for 입력하다 ('to input', technically correct but stiff/office-style) or invent 내비 해 주세요 (vague, not natural). The address particle is 내비에 ('into the nav', destination-of-content): 내비에 주소(를) 찍어 주세요. Useful partners: 켜다 ('turn on'), 끄다 ('turn off'), 내비대로 ('according to the nav'). Register: 찍어 주세요 to a passenger or anyone polite; 찍어 줘 to a friend. Beware: 찍다 also means 'to take a photo/stamp,' so context matters — near a GPS screen, it clearly means 'enter/tap.'

structuredNuance.t: 내비 (clipped from 내비게이션 'navigation/GPS') + 좀 (softener) + 찍다 ('to tap/punch in') + 주세요 — 'please punch the destination into the GPS.' 찍다's core is 'to press/stamp'; on a screen it means 'tap in, enter'. Particle: 내비에 ('into the nav') for the address destination — 내비에 주소 찍어 주세요.

Said to a passenger while you're driving and can't safely operate the screen. 좀 makes it a soft favor request. To a friend: 내비 좀 찍어 줘. Without 좀 it sounds more direct: 내비 찍어 주세요. The full form 내비게이션 is fine but 내비 is universal and preferred in speech.

찍다 ('tap in', casual/natural) vs 입력하다 ('to input', stiff/formal). Don't use 내비 해 주세요 — 하다 is too vague here; you need 찍다 ('tap in the destination') or 켜다 ('turn it on'). 내비대로 가다 ('go according to the nav') is the partner phrase once the destination is set.
내비 좀 찍어 주세요 → 내비에 주소(를) 찍어 주세요 → 목적지 찍어 주세요. Others: 내비 켜 주세요 (turn it on) / 내비 꺼 주세요 (turn it off) / 내비대로 가면 돼요 (just follow the nav).

Two traps: (1) 찍다 is not obvious — English speakers try 입력하다 (too formal) or 내비 해 주세요 (too vague); learn 찍다 as the natural GPS-entry verb. (2) Wrong particle: 내비를 찍어 주세요 sounds like tapping the device itself; you want 내비에 (주소를) 찍어 주세요 — into the nav.

mistakes: Saying 내비 입력해 주세요 in casual speech.
입력하다 ('to input') is technically correct but sounds stiff/technical. Everyday Korean uses 찍다: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 내비를 찍어 주세요 for the destination.
You punch the address INTO the nav: 내비에 (주소를) 찍어 주세요. 내비를 찍다 sounds like you're physically tapping the device body, not entering a destination.
Inventing 내비 해 주세요.
내비 ('navigation') isn't used with 하다 as a verb here. To set it, use 찍다 ('punch in') or 켜다 ('turn on'): 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 / 내비 켜 주세요.

usage: Polite; explaining that transit has stopped for the night — the line is no longer running
반말, to a friend — often realizing too late that service has ended
Asking ahead of time so you don't miss it — the preventive question
Guess I'll have to take a taxi
The consequence — falling back on 택시 after missing the 막차; natural follow-up
examples: 벌써 막차 끊겼어요.
The last train's already gone.
벌써 ('already') adds a sense that it left sooner than hoped or expected
A: 지하철 막차 끊겼어요. 택시 타야겠어요. / B: 카카오택시 불러 드릴게요.
A: The last subway is gone. I'll have to grab a taxi. / B: Let me call a Kakao Taxi for you.
지하철 ('subway') + pivot to 택시; 카카오택시 부르다 ('call Kakao Taxi') is what most people do after midnight
막차 몇 시예요? 놓치면 안 돼요.
What time's the last one? I can't miss it.
놓치다 ('to miss') — the verb for missing a bus, train, or opportunity; -면 안 돼요 for 'must not'
nuance: 막차 끊겼어요 is 막차 ('the last bus/train of the day', 막 'final/last' + 車 'vehicle') + 끊기다 ('to be cut off / stop running') in polite past, 'the last ride has stopped for the night.' The idiom is 끊기다 — the passive of 끊다 ('to cut') — used idiomatically for a service ending: 막차가 끊기다 literally 'the last vehicle gets cut,' meaning it's no longer running. This is one of the most practically important transport phrases in Korea, since subways stop around midnight and you must either catch the 막차 or take a taxi. Contrast 막차 (last departure) with 첫차 ('the first bus/train of the day', 첫 'first'). To say you missed it: 막차 놓쳤어요 (놓치다 = 'to miss/let slip'). The English-speaker trap is saying 막차 떠났어요 ('the last bus departed'), calquing 'the last bus left' — understandable but not the idiomatic Korean; 끊기다 ('service is cut') is about the LINE stopping, not one vehicle leaving. Also, the fixed compound is 막차 (not 마지막차) — 마지막 차 is understandable but 막차 is the natural word. Don't confuse 끊기다 ('be cut off, of service or a call') with transitive 끊다 ('to cut/hang up/quit'): 막차 끊었어요 would wrongly imply someone cut the service.

structuredNuance.t: 막차 ('last bus/train of the day', 막 'final' + 車 'vehicle') + 끊기다 (passive 'to be cut off') in polite past — the service is cut, the night's last ride is no longer running. 끊기다 is the passive of 끊다 ('to cut'); the LINE stops, not just one vehicle. Korea's subways typically stop near midnight, making this phrase genuinely urgent.

Said late at night when realizing transit has stopped. Polite 끊겼어요 to anyone; 끊겼어 (반말) to friends. Often followed by a plan: 택시 타야겠어요 or 카카오택시 불러야겠어요. Preventive question: 막차 몇 시예요? — ask this before leaving the venue, not after.

막차 끊겼어요 ('service is cut') vs 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last one' — 놓치다 'to miss/let slip') vs 막차 떠났어요 ('the last one departed' — possible but not idiomatic). Contrast 막차 (last) with 첫차 ('first bus/train', 첫 'first'). 끊기다 (passive, service stops) vs 끊다 (transitive, someone cuts it).
막차 끊겼어요 → 막차 놓쳤어요 → 이미 막차 지났어요 ('the last one has already passed'). Question: 막차 몇 시예요? / 막차 아직 있어요? ('is there still a last train?').

Two traps: (1) 막차 떠났어요 — calquing 'the last bus left'; 끊기다 is the idiomatic verb meaning the LINE is cut/done, not just one bus left. (2) 막차 끊었어요 (transitive 끊다) — wrongly implies someone cut the service; use passive 끊기다.

mistakes: Saying 막차 떠났어요 for 'last train's gone'.
Koreans idiomatically use 끊기다 ('service is cut off') for transit ending: 막차 끊겼어요. 떠났어요 ('it departed') is understandable but not the lived-in phrase.
Saying 마지막차 instead of 막차.
The fixed word for the night's final bus/train is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). 마지막 차 is understandable but 막차 is the natural compound Koreans actually say.
Using 끊다 instead of 끊기다.
끊다 is transitive ('to cut/hang up/quit'). The last train STOPPING on its own is passive 끊기다: 막차 끊겼어요. 막차 끊었어요 would mean someone deliberately cut the service.

hangul: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요
english: I just got my license recently
usage: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요
Polite; warning passengers or other drivers that you are a new driver — a natural pre-emptive disclosure
면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어
반말, to friends when explaining your cautious or slow driving
초보운전 ('beginner driver') — the sticker label new drivers in Korea put on their car
The basic factual statement — you hold a 운전면허; used when asked, not for self-deprecation
examples: 저 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요. 천천히 갈게요.
I just got my license, so I'll drive slowly.
Set expectations honestly, then 천천히 가다 ('drive slowly') as the natural follow-through
면허 딴 지 얼마 안 돼서 고속도로는 무서워요.
I just got licensed, so highways scare me.
고속도로 ('expressway/highway') is the intimidating part for new drivers; -어서 gives the reason
A: 면허 딴 지 한 달밖에 안 됐어요. 아직 초보예요. / B: 괜찮아요, 천천히 가도 돼요.
A: It's only been a month since I got my license. Still a beginner. / B: That's fine, you can take it slow.
밖에 + 안 됐다 ('only … has passed') stresses how new it is; 천천히 가도 돼요 ('it's OK to go slowly') is the reassuring reply
nuance: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 면허 ('license', 免許; full form 운전면허 = driver's license) + 따다 ('to obtain/earn', the verb for GETTING a certificate) + -ㄴ 지 ('since [doing]') + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has passed'), i.e. 'it hasn't been long since I got my license.' Two idioms to master: (1) 면허를 따다 — you 따다 ('pluck/earn') a license by passing a test, NOT 받다 ('receive') or 가지다 ('have'); 따다 captures the achievement of passing. (2) -은 지 + 얼마 안 됐다 is the fixed frame for 'I recently started X' — this 지 is the time-elapsed noun (always written with a space, attached to a past-style -ㄴ/은 form), completely different from the conjunctive ending -ㄹ지 ('whether'). The culturally vital partner phrase is 초보운전 ('beginner driver'), the label new Korean drivers attach to their car as a courtesy sticker so other drivers give them more patience. The English-speaker trap is the elapsed-time construction — using 동안 ('during') instead of -은 지 for 'since I got it.' To a friend, 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어. Don't confuse 면허 ('driving license/permit') with 자격증 (a professional skills certificate) — driving is specifically 운전면허.

structuredNuance.t: 면허 ('license', 免許) + 따다 ('to earn/get by passing a test') + -ㄴ 지 ('since doing') + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has passed') — 'it hasn't been long since I earned my license.' 따다 captures passing the test; 받다/가지다 do not. -은 지 + 됐어요 is the fixed elapsed-time frame.

A natural disclosure to passengers or when chatting with other drivers to explain cautious driving. Polite 됐어요 to most people; 됐어 (반말) to friends. Cultural note: many Korean new drivers put a 초보운전 sticker on their car — this phrase is the spoken equivalent.

저 초보운전이에요 ('I'm a beginner driver') is a direct label. 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is more specific and conversational, giving the actual time frame. Don't confuse 면허 ('driver's license') with 자격증 (a professional skills certificate) — the driving-specific term is 운전면허.
면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 → 면허 딴 지 한 달밖에 안 됐어요 ('only a month') → 면허 딴 지 일 년도 안 됐어요. Also: 처음 혼자 운전하는 거예요 ('first time driving alone').
chips: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요
면허 딴 지 한 달 됐어요

structuredNuance.t: Two traps: (1) 면허 받았어요 — a license is earned by passing; use 따다, not 받다. (2) Using 동안 ('during') for elapsed time — the correct structure is -은 지 + 됐어요 ('it has been [time] since…'), not 동안 ('during/for a period'). Also, the time-elapsed 지 (written with a space) is NOT the same as the conjunctive ending -ㄹ지 ('whether').

mistakes: Saying 면허 받았어요 instead of 면허 땄어요.
A license is obtained with 따다 ('to earn/win', as in passing a test): 면허(를) 땄어요. 받다 ('receive') sounds like it was simply handed to you without effort.
Using 동안 instead of -은 지 for elapsed time.
'It hasn't been long since I got it' uses -은 지 ... 됐어요: 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요. 동안 ('during/for') is for an ongoing duration — 한 달 동안 ('for a month') — not time-since-an-event.
Confusing the time 지 with the ending -ㄹ지.

딴 지 ('since getting it') is the spaced time-noun 지 after a past form. -ㄹ지 ('whether') is a verb ending, e.g. 갈지 (whether to go). They look alike in text but serve entirely different grammatical roles.

usage: Polite imperative; warning a driver to stay within the speed limit
반말, to a close friend driving — a direct but casual warning
Gentler — nudging for a slower pace without explicitly naming speeding as a violation
Indirect cue — naming the camera lets the driver decide; 단속 카메라 = enforcement camera
examples: 과속하지 마세요. 위험해요.
Don't speed — it's dangerous.
Pair with 위험하다 ('to be dangerous') to give the reason, not just the rule
여기 어린이 보호구역이에요. 과속하지 마세요.
This is a school zone. Don't speed.
어린이 보호구역 ('child protection zone') — fines are doubled and police actively patrol here
A: 앞에 과속 카메라 있어요, 속도 줄이세요. / B: 아, 몰랐어요. 고마워요.
A: Speed camera ahead — slow down. / B: Ah, didn't see it. Thanks.
속도 줄이다 ('reduce speed') is the actionable instruction; 과속 카메라 = speed enforcement camera
nuance: 과속하지 마세요 is 과속 ('speeding', 過 'excess' + 速 'speed') + 하다 (making it the verb 과속하다 'to speed') + -지 마세요 (the polite prohibitive, from 말다 'to stop/refrain'), 'please don't speed.' The grammar pattern -지 마세요 is the standard polite 'don't do X' in Korean — a top learner error is negating with 안: 과속 안 하세요 means 'you don't speed' (a description/statement), not the command 'don't speed.' For prohibitions, -지 마세요 is the form to use. Korea enforces speed limits hard: 단속 카메라 / 과속 카메라 (speed cameras) are common on expressways and urban roads, 어린이 보호구역 (school zones, 시속 30km) carry doubled fines, and 벌금/과태료 are steep. A softer alternative to 과속하지 마세요 is 천천히 가세요 ('drive slowly') or 속도 줄이세요 ('reduce speed'), which nudge rather than prohibit. The English-speaker trap is also calquing 'don't drive fast' as 빨리 운전하지 마세요 — understandable but 과속하다 is the precise, sign-matching term. Don't confuse 과속 (過速 'excessive speed') with 가속 (加速 'acceleration') — one letter apart, opposite intent. To a friend, 과속하지 마.

structuredNuance.t: 과속 ('speeding', 過速 'excess speed') + 하다 (verb) + -지 마세요 (polite prohibitive, from 말다 'to refrain') — 'please don't speed.' -지 마세요 is the standard polite 'don't do X' pattern. Korea enforces speed limits heavily: 단속 카메라 / 과속 카메라, doubled fines in 어린이 보호구역 (school zones, speed limit 시속 30km).

Said by a passenger warning a driver, or as a general instruction. Polite 마세요 to any driver. 마 (반말) to close friends. Softer nudges: 천천히 가세요 (gentle), 속도 좀 줄여 주세요 (polite favor). 과속하지 마세요 is direct — use it when there is real risk or enforcement nearby.

과속하지 마세요 (direct prohibition) vs 천천히 가세요 (gentle nudge) vs 속도 줄이세요 (action instruction). Don't confuse 과속 (過速 'excessive speed = speeding') with 가속 (加速 'acceleration') — 가속하다 means 'to speed up' neutrally; 과속하다 means 'to exceed the limit.'
과속하지 마세요 → 제발 과속하지 마세요 ('please, please don't speed') → 속도 좀 줄여 주세요. Informational: 여기 단속 카메라 있어요 / 어린이 보호구역이에요.

Two traps: (1) 과속 안 하세요 — this is a statement ('you don't speed'), not a command; use -지 마세요 for a prohibition. (2) 빨리 운전하지 마세요 — understandable but 과속하다 is the precise term matching road signs, fines, and cameras.

mistakes: Saying 과속 안 하세요 to mean 'don't speed'.
안 + verb negates a statement ('you don't speed'). A command 'don't do X' is -지 마세요: 과속하지 마세요. This is the core prohibition pattern and applies to all verbs.
Mixing up 과속 and 가속.
과속 ('excessive speed/speeding') is the violation; 가속 ('acceleration') is neutrally speeding up. 가속하지 마세요 would oddly mean 'don't accelerate'. Use 과속 for the speeding warning.
Saying 빨리 운전하지 마세요.
It's understandable but the exact, enforcement-aware term is 과속하다. 과속하지 마세요 matches the signs, cameras, and tickets you'll actually encounter; it sounds like you know the law.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking the parking fee at a lot, booth, or building — the basic cost check
반말, to a friend who might know the lot or has parked there before
More formal; 주차 요금 ('parking charge') with 어떻게 돼요 — used when calling ahead or on a booking form
Asking the per-unit rate when the lot is metered — 에 here means 'per'
examples: 여기 주차비 얼마예요?
How much is parking here?
Asked at the booth or to staff before committing to park; 여기 ('here') specifies this particular lot
주차비 얼마예요? 식당 이용하면 할인돼요?
How much is parking? Is there a discount if I eat here?
할인되다 ('to be discounted') — many Korean lots validate free hours or give discounts for customers
A: 주차비 얼마예요? / B: 30분에 천 원이에요, 초과되면 10분에 오백 원이고요.
A: How much is parking? / B: It's 1,000 won per 30 min, then 500 won per 10 min after that.
초과되다 ('to exceed the included time') is the key word — know it to understand the rate structure
nuance: 주차비 얼마예요? is 주차비 ('parking fee', 주차 + 費 'cost/fee') + 얼마예요 ('how much is it?'), the basic question for a paid lot. The suffix -비 (費) is a productive Sino-Korean fee-marker you'll meet throughout driving: 주차비 (parking), 주유비 / 기름값 (fuel cost), but note 통행료 (toll) uses -료, not -비 — a detail worth fixing. A slightly more formal variant is 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? (요금 = 'charge/rate'); 얼마예요? is the warm everyday choice. Practically, the smart follow-up after learning the fee is 혹시 할인돼요? or 무료예요? — many Korean lots offer customer validation (영수증 validation, 식당 stamp) or free hours for building users. For per-time rates, use the pattern 30분에 얼마예요? (에 = 'per' for rate). The English-speaker trap is using 가격 ('price', for goods you buy) for a service fee — a parking CHARGE is 주차비 or 요금, not 주차 가격; 가격 sounds like a price tag on a product. Another trap: 비 in 주차비 is the fee suffix, not the word for rain (비) — same hangul, different word. With a friend, 주차비 얼마야?

structuredNuance.t: 주차비 ('parking fee', 주차 + 費 'cost/fee') + 얼마예요 ('how much is it?') — a direct cost question. -비 (費) is the fee suffix: 주차비 (parking), 주유비 (fuel), 입장비 (entry). Note 통행료 (toll) uses 료, not 비 — these are different Sino-Korean charge words. For per-time rates: 30분에 얼마예요? (에 = 'per').

Asked at a lot booth, via intercom, or to building staff before parking. Polite 예요 to staff or strangers. To a friend who's been there: 주차비 얼마야? More formal 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? for calling ahead. Smart follow-up: 혹시 할인돼요? or 무료예요?

주차비 얼마예요? (simple cost check) vs 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? (asks for the full rate structure). Distinguish 주차비 (parking fee) from 통행료 (highway toll, uses 료) and 주유비/기름값 (fuel cost). Don't confuse 주차비 (cost) with 주차장 (the lot itself).
주차비 얼마예요? → 주차비 무료예요? → 혹시 할인돼요? → 30분에 얼마예요? → 영수증 가져오면 할인돼요?

The trap is using 가격 ('price', for goods) for a service fee — a parking CHARGE is 주차비 or 요금, not 주차 가격; 가격 is the tag on something you buy. Also: 비 in 주차비 is the Sino-Korean fee suffix (費), not the word for 'rain' (비) — same hangul, different word.

mistakes: Saying 주차 가격 얼마예요?
가격 is the price of goods. A service charge like parking is 주차비 or 주차 요금. 주차 가격 sounds like you're asking the 'price' of parking as if it were a product for sale.
Confusing 통행료 with 주차비.
Both are driving costs, but 통행료 is a road TOLL (uses 료) and 주차비 is a PARKING fee (uses 비). Ask 통행료 얼마예요? at a tollgate, 주차비 얼마예요? at a lot.
Not asking about validation/free time.
Many Korean lots are free or discounted for customers. After 주차비 얼마예요?, ask 무료예요? or 할인돼요? — and specifically 영수증 가져오면 할인돼요? ('discount if I bring a receipt?') at restaurants.

usage: Is it not OK to park here?
Polite question; checking whether parking is forbidden — the negative phrasing implies you suspect it might not be allowed
The positive version — asking permission directly; more neutral than the negative form
반말, telling a friend the spot is off-limits
Stating the rule matter-of-factly — 주차 금지 ('parking prohibited') is the sign language
examples: 여기 주차해도 돼요?
Is it OK to park here?
The everyday way to ask permission before leaving your car — use BEFORE parking, not after
여기 주차하면 안 돼요. 견인돼요.
You can't park here — they'll tow it.
견인되다 ('to be towed', passive) is the consequence; 견인 is a real risk in Korean cities
A: 잠깐 세우는 것도 안 돼요? / B: 네, 여기 주차 금지예요. 앞에 세우세요.
A: Not even for a moment? / B: No, it's a no-parking zone. Pull up ahead.
주차 금지 ('no parking') applies even to brief stops at many designated spots; 앞에 세우세요 gives an alternative
nuance: 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? is 여기 ('here') + 주차하다 ('to park') + -면 안 돼요 ('it's not OK if'), literally 'is it not OK if I park here?' — a polite check on whether parking is forbidden, with the negative phrasing implying you suspect it might not be. This is the entry point to the most important 되다 grammar pair in Korean: -아/어도 돼요? ('may I? is it OK to?', asking PERMISSION) vs -(으)면 안 돼요 ('it's not allowed / you mustn't', a PROHIBITION). So 주차해도 돼요? = 'can I park?'; 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you can't park.' Mixing these is the single biggest 돼요 error for learners. In Korea illegal parking is actively enforced: 불법 주차 (illegal parking), 견인 (towing, very common in Seoul), 주차 금지 (no-parking zones), and 과태료 (fines). Note that 안 돼요 comes from 되다, so it's spelled 돼요, never 되요. Also note 주차하다 can take 에 for the spot: 여기에 주차해도 돼요?, though 여기 alone is fine in speech. To a friend, 여기 주차하면 안 돼. Don't confuse 안 돼요 ('not allowed', from 되다) with 안 해요 ('don't do', from 하다).

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 주차하다 ('to park') + -면 안 돼요 ('it's not OK if') — 'is it not OK to park here?' The negative framing implies you already suspect it might be forbidden. 안 돼요 comes from 되다, so it's spelled 돼요 (= 되어요), NEVER 되요.

Ask staff, a guard, or any nearby person before leaving your car in an uncertain spot. Polite with 안 돼요?; 반말 안 돼 to friends. The positive permission form 주차해도 돼요? is equally natural and slightly more neutral. In Korea, towing (견인) is common in cities, so asking before parking is genuinely important.

Critical pair: -아/어도 돼요? (asking permission, 'may I?') vs -(으)면 안 돼요 (prohibition, 'it's not allowed'). 주차해도 돼요? = 'can I park?' / 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you can't park.' These are not interchangeable — confusing them reverses the meaning entirely. Also don't say 허락돼요? — too formal for parking; use the -도 돼요/-면 안 돼요 patterns.
여기 주차해도 돼요? (positive ask) → 주차하면 안 돼요 (statement of prohibition) → 주차 금지예요 (the rule) → 주차하면 견인돼요 (the consequence).
The biggest -돼요 error: confusing -도 돼요? (permission) with -면 안 돼요 (prohibition). They are opposite patterns. Also: 안 돼요 is spelled with 돼, not 되 — write 주차하면 안 돼요, not 안 되요.

mistakes: Confusing -도 돼요? (permission) with -면 안 돼요 (prohibition).
주차해도 돼요? = 'may I park?'; 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you mustn't park.' Use the right frame: to ask permission, -도 돼요?; to state a ban, -면 안 돼요.
Saying 주차 허락돼요?
허락 ('formal permission/consent') is too heavy for parking. Use the everyday 주차해도 돼요? ('is it OK to park?') instead.
Writing 안 돼요 as 안 되요.
From 되다, the correct contracted form is 돼요 (되어요 → 돼요). 되요 is a common misspelling. So it's 주차하면 안 돼요.

usage: Polite; reporting a small fender-bender to a passenger, friend, or insurance — the go-to phrase for a light contact accident
반말, to a close friend — often texted right after a minor bump
The general version — 사고 ('accident') of any severity; use this if you're not sure or it's more serious
I need to call the insurance company
The next immediate step — calling your 보험 회사 to the scene is standard in Korea
examples: 주차하다가 접촉사고 났어요.
I had a fender-bender while parking.
-다가 ('while in the middle of') shows the accident occurred during the action of parking — not before or after
접촉사고 났어요. 많이 안 다쳤어요, 차만 살짝 긁혔어요.
Had a small collision. No one's seriously hurt — just a scratch on the car.
긁히다 ('to get scratched', passive) for minor paint or body damage; 살짝 ('slightly/lightly') scales it down
A: 접촉사고 났는데 어떻게 해야 돼요? 보험 부를까요? / B: 네, 일단 사진 찍고 보험 부르세요.
A: I had a fender-bender — what should I do? Should I call insurance? / B: Yes, first take photos and then call insurance.
보험 부르다 ('call insurance to the scene') + 사진 찍다 ('take photos') are the standard first two steps
nuance: 접촉사고 났어요 is 접촉사고 ('contact accident/fender-bender', 접촉 'contact' 接觸 + 사고 'accident' 事故) + 나다 ('to occur/happen') in polite past, 'a fender-bender occurred.' The core idiom is 사고(가) 나다 — accidents 나다 ('occur/happen/break out'), an intransitive spontaneous event verb — so you do NOT say 사고를 했어요 ('I did an accident') or 사고를 가졌어요 ('I had an accident'), both calques from English 'have an accident.' Events like accidents, fires, and emergencies all use 나다: 불이 나다 ('a fire breaks out'), 문제가 나다. 접촉사고 specifically means a light scrape or contact — contrast it with 추돌 ('rear-end collision') and 충돌 ('crash/head-on') for more serious accidents. Culturally, after a fender-bender in Korea the standard sequence is: (1) 사진 찍다 ('take photos of the damage'), (2) 보험 부르다 ('call your insurance company to the scene'), (3) 교통경찰 부르다 if there's an injury. Saying 충돌했어요 for a tiny bump is too strong. To a friend, 접촉사고 났어. Don't confuse 사고 ('accident') with 사거리 ('intersection') — similar sound but unrelated.

structuredNuance.t: 접촉사고 ('contact accident/fender-bender', 接觸事故) + 나다 ('to occur/happen', intransitive spontaneous-event verb) in polite past. 사고가 나다 is the fixed idiom — accidents 나다 like fires (불이 나다) and problems; they are events that OCCUR, not things you DO or HAVE. Do NOT use 하다 or 가지다.

Reported to passengers, friends, or insurance right after a minor collision. Polite 났어요 to most people; 났어 to close friends (often via text). The professional register when calling insurance: 접촉사고가 발생했어요 ('a contact accident has occurred', 발생하다 = 'to arise'). But in everyday speech, 났어요 is universal.

접촉사고 (light contact/scrape) vs 추돌 ('rear-end collision', more serious) vs 충돌 ('crash', severe) vs 사고 (any accident, general). Use 접촉사고 for the smallest category. Don't confuse 사고 ('accident') with 사거리 ('intersection') — they rhyme but are unrelated.
접촉사고 났어요 → 사고 났어요 (general) → 사고가 발생했어요 (formal/professional). Post-accident steps: 사진 찍으세요 → 보험 부르세요 → 경찰 부르세요 (if injury).

Two traps: (1) 사고를 했어요 / 사고를 가졌어요 — calquing 'have an accident'; accidents 나다 (occur), not 하다/가지다. (2) 충돌했어요 for a tiny scrape — 충돌 is a serious crash; save it for real impact. Use 접촉사고 났어요 for a fender-bender.

mistakes: Saying 사고를 했어요 or 사고 가졌어요.
Accidents 나다 ('occur'), not 하다/가지다. The correct frame is 사고(가) 났어요 / 접촉사고 났어요. English 'have an accident' doesn't translate literally into Korean.
Using 충돌했어요 for a tiny scrape.
충돌 ('crash/collision') is strong and implies serious impact. A minor bump is 접촉사고 ('contact accident'). Save 충돌했어요 for a real crash; say 접촉사고 났어요 for a fender-bender.
Calling only the police, not insurance.
In Korea you typically 보험 부르다 ('call your insurance to the scene') for fender-benders, often before calling police. Saying 접촉사고 났어요 and asking 보험 부를까요? is the normal next move.

usage: Polite-neutral; checking the turn with a passenger or checking what the GPS said
반말, to a friend navigating — quick confirmation mid-drive
Is it a right turn here?
The right-turn version — 우회전 ('right turn'); double-check before committing
Turn left at the next intersection
Giving the instruction to a driver; 사거리 ('intersection') as a clear landmark
examples: 여기서 좌회전해요?
Do I turn left here?
Asked at a junction when you're unsure — the uncertainty turns the statement into a rising-intonation question
여기서 좌회전해요, 아니면 직진해요?
Do I turn left here, or go straight?
직진하다 ('to go straight', 直進) as the clear alternative; 아니면 ('or') for a binary choice
A: 여기서 좌회전하면 안 돼요, 비보호예요. 신호 받고 가세요. / B: 아, 몰랐어요. 고마워요.
A: You can't just turn left here — it's an unprotected turn. Wait for the green arrow. / B: Ah, I didn't know. Thanks.
비보호 (좌회전) = 'unprotected left turn' — turn only when safe or on a dedicated arrow signal; foreigners get fined misjudging these
nuance: 여기서 좌회전해요? is 여기서 ('here', 여기 + 에서 contracted to 서 'at this point') + 좌회전하다 ('to turn left', 左 'left' + 回轉 'rotation') + 해요? (polite question), 'do I turn left here?' The four essential driving directions are Sino-Korean: 좌회전 (left turn), 우회전 (right turn), 직진 (straight, 直進), and 유턴 (U-turn, English loan). These are exactly the words your GPS (내비) says and the road signs show — memorize them as a set. The particle is 에서 (spoken as 서) because the turn is an action performed AT that location, not a destination you arrive at: 여기서 좌회전해요. Using 에 instead — 여기에 좌회전해요 — is a learner error. In Korea, a critical cultural vocabulary item is 비보호 좌회전 ('unprotected left turn'): you must either have a dedicated green-arrow signal or turn only when oncoming lanes are completely clear; foreigners misread this constantly and get fines. The English-speaker trap beyond the particle is using plain 돌다 ('to turn/spin') as 왼쪽으로 돌아요? — understandable informally but 좌회전하다 is the precise, sign-matching verb. To a friend, 여기서 좌회전해?

structuredNuance.t: 여기서 ('here', from 에서 'at this point') + 좌회전하다 ('to turn left', 左回轉) + 해요? — 'do I turn left here?' The particle 에서/서 marks where the action happens (NOT 에, which marks a destination). The four driving directions to know: 좌회전 / 우회전 / 직진 / 유턴 — the same words your GPS speaks.

Asked mid-drive to a passenger or checked against the GPS. Polite 해요? to any passenger. 반말 해? to a friend navigating. When giving the instruction to a driver: 여기서 좌회전하세요 (polite imperative) or 좌회전이에요 (factual announcement).

좌회전 (left) vs 우회전 (right) vs 직진 (straight) vs 유턴 (U-turn) — the four GPS/sign terms. Key cultural item: 비보호 좌회전 = 'unprotected left turn', where you turn only when clear or on a dedicated arrow — missing this causes fines. 왼쪽으로 돌아요? is informal but 좌회전하다 matches signs and nav.
여기서 좌회전해요? → 여기서 좌회전이에요? → 다음 사거리에서 좌회전하세요. Opposite: 여기서 우회전해요? / 직진해요?

Two traps: (1) Using 에 instead of 에서/서 for the turn location — a turn is an action AT a point (에서), not a destination (에): say 여기서 좌회전해요? (2) Saying 왼쪽으로 돌아요? — informal and imprecise; 좌회전하다 is the driving-specific verb matching road signs and your nav.

mistakes: Using 에 instead of 에서/서 for the turn location.
A turn is an action performed AT a place, so use 에서 (spoken 서): 여기서 좌회전해요? 여기에 좌회전 is wrong — 에 marks a destination, not where an action happens.
Saying 왼쪽으로 돌아요? for a driving turn.
돌다 ('to spin/turn around') is loose and imprecise for driving. The exact driving verb is 좌회전하다, matching road signs and your nav: 여기서 좌회전해요?
Confusing 좌회전 (left) with 우회전 (right).
좌 = left (左), 우 = right (右). Swapping them reverses your route. Lock in 좌회전/우회전/직진/유턴 as the four driving directions as a set.

usage: Polite; directing a driver to the electronic-toll lane on an expressway
반말, to a friend driving — a quick directional cue as you approach the tollgate
No Hi-Pass? Take the regular lane
일반 차로 ('regular/general lane') where you pay cash or card at a staffed or card-only booth
통행료 ('toll fee', 通行料) + 내다 ('to pay') — explaining the payment point at a manned booth
examples: 하이패스 있어요? 그럼 하이패스로 가세요.
Got Hi-Pass? Then take the Hi-Pass lane.
First check for the device (있어요?), then direct them — this is the complete two-step exchange
하이패스로 가세요. 안 멈춰도 돼요.
Take the Hi-Pass lane — you don't have to stop.
안 멈춰도 되다 ('don't need to stop') captures the whole point of Hi-Pass; the gate opens automatically
A: 하이패스 단말기 없어서 일반 차로로 가야 돼요. 통행료 현금으로 내도 돼요? / B: 네, 아니면 카드로도 돼요.
A: No Hi-Pass unit, so I have to use the regular lane. Can I pay the toll in cash? / B: Yes, or card works too.
단말기 ('the transponder unit') + 통행료 by 현금 ('cash') or 카드 ('card'); both are accepted at 일반 차로 booths
nuance: 하이패스로 가세요 is 하이패스 ('Hi-Pass', Korea's electronic toll-collection brand/system) + 로 ('via/by way of', the means-and-route particle) + 가세요 ('please go'), 'go through the Hi-Pass lane.' Hi-Pass is a prepaid RFID transponder (단말기 'unit') with a chip card that lets you pass tollgates at low speed without stopping; without it you use a 일반 차로 ('regular lane') and pay 통행료 (通行料 'toll', note 료 not 비) by cash or card. The particle 로/으로 marks the route or means — a high-frequency pattern: 이쪽으로 가세요 ('go this way'), 카드로 내다 ('pay by card'). A top learner error is using 에 or 에서 — 하이패스로 가다 means 'go VIA the Hi-Pass lane', which is correct; 하이패스에 가다 would sound like going TO a place called Hi-Pass. Practically, if your Hi-Pass card runs out of balance it beeps and the gate may not open, potentially causing a rear-end situation — top it up at a 편의점 or 주유소. The English-speaker trap is treating 하이패스 as just a card; in Korean 하이패스 names the entire lane and system, so 하이패스로 가세요 is the natural instruction. To a friend, 하이패스로 가. Distinguish 통행료 (highway toll) from 주차비 (parking fee) and 주유비 (fuel cost).

structuredNuance.t: 하이패스 (Korea's electronic-toll system/lane) + 로 ('via/by way of', means-and-route particle) + 가세요 ('please go') — 'go through the Hi-Pass lane.' 하이패스 uses a RFID transponder (단말기) + chip card; gate opens automatically at low speed. Without one, use 일반 차로 and pay 통행료 (통行料, note 료 not 비) by cash or card.

Said as you approach an expressway tollgate — either to direct a driver or to tell a friend which lane to use. Polite 가세요; 반말 가 to friends. The opposite instruction: 하이패스 없으면 일반 차로로 가세요. The particle 로 is the key: it marks route/means, a pattern reusable in many situations (이쪽으로, 카드로, 버스로).

하이패스 차로 (Hi-Pass lane) vs 일반 차로 (regular pay lane). 통행료 (highway toll, uses 료) vs 주차비 (parking fee, uses 비) vs 주유비/기름값 (fuel cost) — all driving costs, different words. Don't confuse 차로 ('traffic lane') with 통행료.
하이패스로 가세요 → 하이패스 차로로 가세요 (fuller) → 하이패스 없으면 일반 차로로 가세요. Related: 하이패스 잔액 확인하세요 ('check your Hi-Pass balance'), 하이패스 충전해야 돼요 ('need to top up the Hi-Pass').

Two traps: (1) Using 에/에서 instead of 로 — 하이패스에 가세요 sounds like going TO a place called Hi-Pass; you want 하이패스로 ('via the Hi-Pass lane'). (2) Thinking 하이패스 is just a card — in Korean it names the whole lane/system, so 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass route') is natural and complete.

mistakes: Using 에/에서 instead of 로 for the lane.
To go VIA the Hi-Pass lane you mark the route with 로/으로: 하이패스로 가세요. 하이패스에 가세요 sounds like going TO a place called Hi-Pass, not passing through that lane.
Thinking 하이패스 is only a card.
In Korean 하이패스 names the whole electronic-toll lane/system, not just the card. So 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass lane') is the natural instruction.
Confusing 통행료 (toll) with 주차비/주유비.
통행료 (uses 료) is the highway toll; 주차비 is parking, 주유비/기름값 is fuel. At a tollgate you 통행료(를) 내다 ('pay the toll'), not 주차비.
